title: The Restrictiveness Ladder
blurb: Order the modifiers from most restrictive (top) to least (bottom) — by how much code can reach the member. Note: internal sits beside protected in the middle; the two can't be strictly ranked against each other, so this ladder uses the rest.

glossary.private: The narrowest: only the containing type can touch it.
glossary.private protected: Slightly wider than private — derived types, but only within the same assembly (protected AND internal).
glossary.protected internal: The widest of the protected family — the whole assembly PLUS derived types anywhere (protected OR internal).
glossary.public: The widest of all — any code in any assembly.

levels.title: L1 · The core four
levels.prompt: Most restrictive at the top, least at the bottom.

failStates.title: public is the least restrictive
failStates.explain: public lets any code anywhere in. It belongs at the very bottom of the ladder, not near the top.

failStates.title: private is narrower than private protected
failStates.explain: private is the tightest — only the containing type. private protected adds same-assembly derived types, so it's slightly wider and goes below private.

levels.title: L2 · Slot in protected
levels.prompt: Add protected to the ladder. Most restrictive at the top.

failStates.title: protected internal is wider than protected
failStates.explain: protected internal adds the whole assembly on top of what protected already allows, so it's LESS restrictive — it sits below protected.

failStates.title: private protected is narrower than protected
failStates.explain: private protected restricts protected down to only same-assembly derived types, so it's more restrictive — it goes above protected.

failStates.title: public belongs at the bottom
failStates.explain: public is the least restrictive of all — it always goes last.
